newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Central Bank's outlook for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Central Bank's outlook for 1997.

text.p: * Excerpts from the Central Bank's 1996 year-end report

The strong economic results achieved in 1996 has by now clearly established the ability of the economy to stay on a high growth path without necessarily running into financial imbalances. The qualitative improvement has been brought about by the cumulative impact of policy reforms across a broad front that have opened up the economy to competition, improved administrative capacity, made available more financial resources, and lowered costs of doing business.

Maintaining the reform-oriented and financially prudent policy course will put a 7-8 percent GNP growth rate target in 1997 well within reach. This can be accompanied by average inflation in the range of 6-7 percent as well as further strengthening of the external financial position and build-up in official reserves. Achieving these results means that the Philippines will be able to grow faster than the rate of inflation, a feat that was last achieved in 1987, albeit at a lower level of GNP growth of 4.6 percent.

A more liberal and open trading arrangement as a result of understandings reached in the context of APEC, AFTA, and WTO as well as regional and bilateral trade commitments is expected to provide a favourable environment for rapid export-led Philippine economic growth.

As chief guardian of financial stability, the BSP (Central Bank) has to be constantly on guard against destabilising external shocks. While the liberalisation of the economy has opened up multiple opportunities for rapid economic growth, it has also made it more vulnerable to sudden shifts in market sentiment that can cause sudden crisis in the financial and foreign exchange markets. The BSP is therefore committed to acting swiftly and independently to modify monetary policy settings if the situation so warrants. In the past, for example, the BSP has not hesitated to push up interest rates significantly to stem a speculative currency attack.

More fundamentally, the BSP will seek to closely coordinate with other government agencies especially in the areas of improving public sector savings and further reducing distortions in the financial system due to uneven tax and other regulations.

The BSP will also intensify cooperative working arrangements with other central banks to improve access on timely basis to relevant market information as well as to external liquidity to help deal with financial crisis. At present, the BSP maintains excellent central banking contacts through the south East Asian Central Banks (SEACEN) and the Executive Meeting of East Asia and Pacific (EMEAP) fora.

More open capital markets have also created special challenges in banking supervision as banks play a more active role in intermediating foreign capital flows. The BSP, in addition to improving its supervision ability, is therefore taking a more pro-active stance to ensure adequate capitalization of banks as well as the commitment of bank senior management to directly oversee risk management and control systems in their respective organisations.
WHAT THE GOVERNMENT NEEDS TO DO

Finally, in the context of further giving substance to the independence of the BSP to act objectively and pro-actively on economic developments, it is vital that the National Government address decisively the balance of the full capitalization of the BSP, as provided for under Republic Act No. 7653, in the amount of 40 billion pesos. A strong capital base is essential to the continuing ability and credibility of the BSP to do its job well of preserving financial stability.
